calibration.fitted_to: the Ubx arm only (wing traits at 39% of endogenous Ubx)
calibration.arm_held_out: the Antp arm (haltere-like wing at 490% of endogenous Antp)

prediction.note: The two protein-ratio measurements in the SAME paper disagree (18.5x by antibody, 10.5x by matched GFP fusions). That disagreement propagates directly into this prediction and is the dominant source of error in it. Both are reported; neither is preferred here.

sweep.note: W at steady state from a neutral initial condition (W0=0.5) at every cell. Axes are Ubx as a fraction of endogenous T3 Ubx and Antp as a multiple of endogenous T2 Antp.

limitations: This is a cartoon. The real decision involves at least vg, sd, wg, dpp, the EGFR/Ras pathway, sal, SRF/blistered and the achaete-scute complex, all of which Ubx regulates (Weatherbee 1998 PMID 9585507; Mohit 2006 PMID 16414040; Pallavi 2006 PMID 16815386). The model has ONE state variable standing for all of them.

The Hox-dose assumption (Ubx and Antp interchangeable up to a scale factor) is known to be false for distant Hox proteins: Paul et al. show Abd-A rescues the four-winged phenotype and Scr does not. The model would be wrong for Scr.

kx is fitted, so the model cannot be said to predict the Ubx threshold - only the Antp one. With a single fitted parameter and a single held-out number, the test is weak; it would be much stronger against a dose series, which the paper reports qualitatively but not as tabulated numbers I could extract.

Time is nondimensional. gamma=1 sets the unit and the model says nothing about how long the decision actually takes, nor about the fact that Ubx acts at several successive stages of haltere morphogenesis (Pavlopoulos & Akam 2011, PMID 21282633).
The readout W is an abstraction scored against a threshold declared in advance; it is not any measured quantity. Calling W>0.5 'a wing' is a modelling convention, not an observation.

Spatial structure is absent. The real decision happens across a disc with compartment boundaries and a Dpp gradient whose RANGE Ubx controls (Crickmore & Mann 2006, PMID 16741075); a well-mixed ODE cannot represent that, and organ SIZE - which is most of what Ubx does - is outside the model entirely.

bistable.note: Cooperative self-activation (n=4). Parameters were chosen so this variant gets a FAIR test rather than a strawman one: beta is large enough that with Hox repression fully relieved the low state does not exist, so a naive T2 disc ignites into a wing on its own, and wild-type T2 and T3 both sit OUTSIDE the bistable window. It has a genuine bistable window at intermediate Hox dose and therefore predicts hysteresis.

antibody_18.5.kx_fitted_to: Ubx arm only (39% of endogenous Ubx)

gfp_10.5.kx_fitted_to: Ubx arm only (39% of endogenous Ubx)

graded.note: Non-cooperative self-activation (n=1). Has no bistable window at any Hox dose, so it predicts a single-valued, continuous dose-response with intermediate organs at intermediate doses.

antibody_18.5.kx_fitted_to: Ubx arm only (39% of endogenous Ubx)

gfp_10.5.kx_fitted_to: Ubx arm only (39% of endogenous Ubx)

hysteresis_test_model_independent.logic: A hysteretic switch REQUIRES the haltere-to-wing transition to sit at a strictly lower Hox dose than the wing-to-haltere transition. The two published thresholds are measured on opposite branches, so their ordering tests hysteresis directly, with no model in between.
hysteresis_test_model_independent.verdict: Under BOTH protein-ratio measurements the ordering is the one a hysteretic switch forbids: the haltere-to-wing dose is the HIGHER of the two. Under the GFP ratio the two doses are within 4% of each other, i.e. effectively a single threshold. So the published numbers do not support a bistable switch with a usable hysteresis window, and they are consistent with a graded, single-valued readout of Hox dose - which is also what Paul et al. report qualitatively when they say intermediate Hox levels give intermediate organs.
hysteresis_test_model_independent.caveat: The two thresholds were scored on different traits (wing veins, hairs and flattening appearing in a haltere; size, shape and hair organisation making a wing resemble a haltere) and in different tissues. They are not two readings of one instrument, so a modest disagreement between them is expected and the 4% agreement under the GFP ratio should not be over-read.

post_hoc_verification.added_by: the agent that completed the page, after study 1 was built
post_hoc_verification.what_was_checked: Study 1 depends on four numbers attributed to Paul et al. 2021 (PMID 34001903). None of them is in that paper's PubMed abstract. The full text is open access and was fetched this session (Europe PMC, PMC8129201; stored at data/paul2021-PMC8129201-fulltext.xml, sha256 4e12dc00acaf5c3d21f2e8690ec56f53646cc3a80b87c656c45dfc56b59c6d92) and all four were confirmed verbatim.

confirmed.39 percent of endogenous Ubx: 'characteristic wing-like phenotypic traits (including veins, hairs organization, and flattening) eventually appeared when the level decreased to 39% of endogenous Ubx (2.5 times lower than endogenous Ubx)'
confirmed.490 percent of endogenous Antp: 'the wing resembled a haltere in terms of size, shape, and hairs organization when the expression level corresponded to 490% of endogenous Antp'
confirmed.18.5x by antibody: 'Ubx was 18.5 times more strongly expressed than Antp'
confirmed.10.5x by GFP: 'Ubx expression levels were 10.5 times higher than Antp levels'

post_hoc_verification.correction_to_this_study_s_framing: This study's `prediction.note` calls the two protein-ratio measurements a disagreement that 'propagates directly' into the prediction. That is true arithmetically, but it understates what the paper says: Paul et al. do not leave the two numbers in conflict. They attribute the gap to antibody affinity and conclude that 'the Antp antibody is 1.85 times less affine', which makes the GFP-based 10.5x their own preferred measurement. The GFP arm is also the arm whose held-out prediction lands within 4%. So the model comparison and the paper's own reasoning select the same number, independently - which is a stronger result than this study originally claimed, not a weaker one.
post_hoc_verification.independent_support_for_the_graded_varia: The paper states directly, of both the Antp and the Ubx series, that 'In both cases, intermediate levels led to intermediary phenotypes'. That is an OBSERVATION of intermediate organs at intermediate doses, which is what this study's graded variant predicts and what its bistable variant forbids. It was not used to build the model and it is not part of the 4% prediction; it is a separate, qualitative confirmation of the variant the quantitative test already selected.
post_hoc_verification.figure_fix: The control figure's y-axis was pinned to (-0.03, 1.05) while the bistable variant's wing branch settles at about 1.61, so that curve ran off the top of the panel and the panel read as a MISSING curve rather than a high one. The axis now follows the data. No model code was changed.
post_hoc_verification.stale_result_found_and_refreshed: The inherited hox-identity.json was NOT the output of the hox_identity.py beside it. Re-running the code unchanged - the only edit was a figure axis limit - moved the bistable variant's held-out prediction from 200 (i.e. it never crossed) to 6.82, flipped controls.all_variants_pass from false to true, rewrote both variant descriptions, and added a whole `hysteresis_test_model_independent` section that no earlier result carried. So the code had been revised and never re-run, and the emitted result described a superseded model. The refreshed result is the one in this file. It is also the better one: the bistable variant now passes the same controls as the graded one, which makes the comparison a fair test rather than a strawman, and the discrimination it reports (4.0% vs 39.2% on the GFP protein ratio) is smaller and more credible than the 40-fold gap the stale file implied.
post_hoc_verification.not_changed: No model code, parameter, control or conclusion was altered by hand. The only edit to hox_identity.py was a figure axis limit; everything else here is that file's own output, refreshed.

Both variants pass: every arm settles past the pre-declared organ-call threshold of W = 0.5 and stays there, and the two starting conditions converge to the same answer, which is what says the wild-type points are not inside a bistable window. The bistable variant's parameters were chosen to make this control pass, so that the sweep is a test of a fair opponent.

Right, the arm that was held out: the vertical line is Paul et al.'s measured 490% of endogenous Antp. On the GFP protein ratio the graded variant crosses the threshold 4.0% away from it and the bistable variant 39.2% away. The dashed and solid pairs on the right are the two protein-ratio measurements reported in that same paper, carried through separately rather than averaged: on the antibody ratio both variants do worse, 68% and 124%, which is the honest shape of this result - the ratio measurement moves the answer by more than the model variant does.

studies.title: How many veins can a wing have, and what sets the number?
studies.question: If you wanted a wing with different venation - more veins, fewer, somewhere else - what kind of knob would you be turning? A reaction-diffusion model is the cheapest way to ask whether vein NUMBER is set by the chemistry's own length scale or by the size of the sheet it runs on, and whether those two give the same answer.
studies.summary: A Gierer-Meinhardt activator-inhibitor system with saturation, run on a wing-blade-shaped domain, with the vein-counting rule declared in the module docstring before the first run and never changed. The inhibitor's diffusivity is not hand-picked: it is solved from the model's own linear stability analysis so that the fastest-growing wavelength would give five longitudinal veins, which makes the count a test of the nonlinear simulation against its own theory. It passes on SPACING and fails by one on COUNT - the measured wavelength matches the prediction to 0.1%, while the counted number falls short by a near-constant one vein across a 2.4-fold range of blade width, which is what two boundaries each suppressing half a wavelength looks like. The honest reading is that blade width is the clean knob and lateral-inhibition range is not: widen the inhibitor's reach much beyond wild type and the pattern breaks up rather than coarsening, so the counting rule goes out of its domain and the small numbers it returns mean 'no stripes' rather than 'fewer veins'. The study's largest weakness is that stripe ORIENTATION is imposed by anisotropic diffusion rather than earned: without that term the same kinetics make labyrinths, and in a real wing the orientation comes from Hedgehog and Dpp positional information laid down before lateral inhibition refines anything. Its second weakness is that NEITHER convergence control passes - the field is still drifting at the end of the run, and at least one seed's vein count still changes in the second half - so part of the reported seed spread is convergence rather than pattern formation, and the runs were deliberately not lengthened until the control passed.

data.headline: Under a counting rule declared before the first run, the model makes 4.0 +/- 0.0 longitudinal veins where its own linear stability analysis predicts 5.0. That deficit is not noise and it is not a one-off: across the blade-width sweep the counted number tracks the predicted number with a near-constant shortfall of 1.0 +/- 0.2 veins, which is the blade's two edges each suppressing a half-wavelength. So the model gets the SPACING right - the measured wavelength matches theory to 0.1% - and the COUNT wrong by one, every time. The lateral-inhibition sweep is messier: widening the inhibitor's reach removes veins one at a time down to about 2.5x wild type, and beyond that the pattern breaks up rather than coarsening, with the seed-to-seed spread exceeding the trend.

model.kind: reaction-diffusion (Gierer-Meinhardt with saturation, anisotropic activator diffusion) on a wing-blade-shaped domain
model.equations: da/dt = div(D_a grad a) + rho a^2 / (h (1 + kappa a^2)) - mu a + rho_0 ;  dh/dt = div(D_h grad h) + rho a^2 - nu h

parameters.name: grid points along the proximodistal axis
parameters.source: Resolution. Checked by C4 and by the wavelength control C3; not a biological quantity.

parameters.name: grid points across the anteroposterior axis
parameters.source: Resolution.

parameters.name: blade aspect ratio (length / maximum width)
parameters.source: A Drosophila wing blade is roughly two and a half times longer than it is wide. Eyeballed from the standard wing diagram, not measured from a specimen, so it is assumed.

parameters.name: position of the counting transect
parameters.source: Declared in the docstring before the first run. Chosen because it is distal to the wing hinge and proximal to the blade tip, so all five longitudinal veins are present there in a real wing.

parameters.name: activator autocatalysis rate
parameters.source: Sets the time unit. Not a measured rate.

parameters.name: activator decay rate
parameters.source: Sets the time unit with RHO.

parameters.name: inhibitor decay rate
parameters.source: Slightly faster than the activator's, which is the usual regime for a stable stripe pattern. Not a measured rate.

parameters.name: basal activator production
parameters.source: A small basal term so the field cannot be trapped at a = 0.

parameters.name: activator saturation
parameters.source: Saturation is what turns a Gierer-Meinhardt spot pattern into a STRIPE pattern. Veins are stripes, so the term is required for the model to be about veins at all. Its value is assumed.

parameters.name: activator diffusivity across the blade
parameters.source: Lengths in this study are grid cells and times are in units of 1/mu. Setting the activator's diffusivity fixes the length unit; every wavelength below is reported in cells and as a fraction of blade width, which is the only form that means anything here.

parameters.name: activator diffusivity along the blade, as a multiple of across
parameters.source: Veins run PROXIMODISTALLY. An isotropic Turing system makes labyrinths, not parallel longitudinal stripes, so something has to orient them. In the animal that something is positional information - Hh and Dpp stripes laid down before lateral inhibition refines them (Crozatier et al. 2003, PMID 12782270). This model has no such prepattern, so the orientation is imposed crudely as anisotropic diffusion. This is the single biggest liberty the study takes and the one a reviewer should attack first.

parameters.name: integration step
parameters.source: Set from the explicit scheme's own stability limit, dt < 1 / (2 (D_x + D_y)) for the fastest-diffusing species, with a safety factor. HISTORY, recorded rather than deleted: the first version of this study used a step 250 times above that limit. It did not visibly blow up, because the code clipped the fields - so it produced a plausible-looking pattern from an unstable integration, and the steady-state control C4 is what caught it.

parameters.name: integration steps
parameters.source: Checked by C4, which requires a pointwise steady state and FAILS, and by C4b, which checks that the readout has converged and passes. Both are reported.

parameters.name: random seeds per condition
parameters.source: Declared as V5 before the first run. A Turing pattern is seed-dependent; one picture is not the measurement.

parameters.name: amplitude of the initial noise
parameters.source: The symmetry-breaking seed. Patterns are reported with their spread across seeds for this reason.

parameters.name: inhibitor diffusivity, wild type
parameters.source: NOT hand-picked. Solved from the linear stability analysis so that the fastest-growing wavelength equals the blade width divided by 5, which is how many longitudinal veins Drosophila has. The nonlinear simulation is then asked whether it agrees, which makes the vein count a test rather than a fit.

model.fitted_to: nothing. The one parameter that could have been fitted - the inhibitor diffusivity - is solved from the linear stability analysis instead, before any count is taken.

counting_criterion.declared: in the module docstring, before the first run
counting_criterion.V1: readout is the activator field at the end of the run
counting_criterion.V2: threshold is the midpoint of the 5th and 95th percentiles, computed per run
counting_criterion.V4: a vein is a run of >= 2 above-threshold pixels with peak prominence >= 10% of the percentile range
counting_criterion.V5: 8 seeds; mean, sd and the per-seed list are all reported

C1_counter_positive_control.history: This control failed on its first run, 5 painted stripes counting as 6 and 9 as 10. The fault was in the CONTROL's own stimulus, not in the counter: the painted field put a peak on both edges of the blade as well as in the interior, so it genuinely had n+1 stripes. The stimulus was corrected and the counter was left untouched. Recorded because a positive control that is debugged until it passes is worth nothing unless you say which side you changed.

C4_steady_state_reached.if_failed: A Turing pattern keeps drifting slowly long after its stripes have stopped moving. The declared threshold is left where it was declared and the failure is reported. Running 4x longer (200,000 steps instead of 50,000) lowered the residual only from 7.6e-3 to 3.8e-3 while leaving the vein count at 4 and the dominant wavelength at 10.00 cells. C4b was added afterwards to ask whether the READOUT had nonetheless converged - and it has not, quite: see C4b.

C4b_readout_converged.what: vein count and dominant wavelength at the half-way point of the run compared with the end
C4b_readout_converged.if_failed: C4b fails too, and the page says so. The vein count is identical between the half-way point and the end for most seeds but not all: at least one seed is still losing or gaining a vein in the second half of the run. So neither the field nor the readout is fully converged at 50,000 steps, the seed spread reported throughout this study is partly a CONVERGENCE spread rather than purely a pattern-formation one, and every count here should be read with that attached. We did not lengthen the runs until it passed, because running to a passing number and then reporting that number is how a control becomes decoration.

controls.all_pass_note: all_pass is false whenever ANY declared control fails, including C4. C4b does not rescue it and is not counted in all_pass.

predicted_minus_counted_veins_over_blade.reading: A near-constant shortfall of about one vein between what linear stability theory predicts and what the nonlinear simulation builds, across a 2.4-fold range of blade width. A constant offset rather than a proportional one is what a boundary effect looks like: the two edges of the blade each suppress about half a wavelength, and that costs one stripe regardless of how many fit in between.

lateral_inhibition_range.knob: inhibitor (Notch/Delta) diffusivity, as a multiple of the wild-type value chosen by linear stability

blade_width.knob: blade aspect ratio, i.e. how wide the wing is at the transect while the patterning chemistry is held fixed. This is the knob Hox dosage turns in study 1: Crickmore & Mann 2006 (PMID 16741075) showed Ubx controls organ SIZE by regulating morphogen production and mobility.

activator_saturation.knob: saturation of the activator's self-activation. At zero the system makes SPOTS rather than stripes, which is a different organ, not a wing with different veins.

limitations: This is a simulation. No wing was imaged and no vein was counted on an animal anywhere in this study.

The mapping from the model's two chemicals to EGFR/rhomboid and Notch/Delta is an analogy, not a derivation. The real vein network is specified by POSITIONAL INFORMATION first - Hh and Dpp place the proveins (Crozatier et al. 2003, PMID 12782270; Sturtevant et al. 1993, PMID 8504935) - and lateral inhibition then refines boundaries. A pure Turing model gets the spacing without the identity, so it can say how MANY veins and not WHICH.
Stripe orientation is imposed by anisotropic diffusion, with an 8-fold ratio that is assumed. Without it the same kinetics make labyrinths. This is the study's largest liberty.

Crossveins are absent from the model entirely. A real Drosophila wing has two of them and they are patterned differently from the longitudinal veins; the counting transect was placed, and declared, to avoid them, which means the model is never tested against the part of the venation it cannot make.

The counts are integers from a thresholded field. Seed spread is reported, but the spread of a count is a crude summary of the spread of a pattern: two runs with the same count can look quite different.

NEITHER convergence control passes. C4, the declared pointwise steady-state check, fails; C4b, added afterwards to ask whether the readout had converged anyway, also fails, because at least one seed's vein count still changes in the second half of the run. Part of the seed spread quoted throughout this study is therefore convergence, not pattern formation, and the runs were deliberately not lengthened until the control passed.

At large inhibitor range the sweep stops being a vein-count sweep at all: the pattern breaks into fragments and the counting rule, which is a rule about stripes, returns small numbers that mean 'no stripes here' rather than 'fewer veins'. The rule was not changed to accommodate that, so those rows should be read as out of the model's domain rather than as measurements.
All parameters except the blade aspect ratio are nondimensional. Nothing in this study is calibrated to a measured concentration, diffusivity or rate, because we found none to calibrate to.

Right, the activator profile along that transect plotted against position across the blade, with the threshold and the prominence criterion drawn as vertical lines and each counted vein shaded

figures.alt: A row of eight simulated blade-shaped activator fields across increasing inhibitor diffusivity, all on one spatial and one intensity scale, each labelled with the mean and standard deviation of vein count over eight seeds, above a matching row of bar charts comparing the counted number against the number linear stability theory predicts

The bold number under each panel is the mean and standard deviation over eight seeds; the image above it is ONE seed and is not the measurement. The black dash on each bar is what the model's own linear stability analysis predicts, and the gap between dash and bar is the roughly one-vein boundary deficit. The three right-hand panels are not 'fewer veins': the pattern has broken up, and a counting rule about stripes has nothing to count.

studies.title: Would four wings fly better? Lift, power, and the organ you spent to get them
studies.question: The design intuition is that more wing area means more lift means better flight. The question this study exists to answer is what that intuition leaves out - and the literature says it leaves out two things, an actuator and a sensor, because the four-winged fly's second pair has only rudimentary flight muscle and the halteres it was made from were rate gyroscopes.
studies.summary: Two coupled models over the same four wing configurations: a quasi-steady blade-element model for lift, power and control authority, and a one-axis attitude model written as a delay-differential equation with saturating control, run with and without the fast haltere feedback loop. One parameter is calibrated - the lift coefficient, set so the two-wing wild type supports exactly body weight - which makes every other configuration a prediction, and all part-A results are ratios so the absolute scale cancels. The result to start from is pure geometry: redistributing the SAME total area over four wings gives 0.46 body weights and does not fly, because lift scales with the second moment of wing area, so splitting one wing into two smaller ones loses more than half of it and no contested biological parameter enters. Adding a second driven pair on top does buy lift, 1.83 body weights at twice the power, while the configuration the literature actually produced reaches 0.84 and stays below 1 across the whole admissible range of the contested fore-hind interference term rather than at one chosen value of it. The control half gives every loop delay the best gain in a swept family and still finds that no loop slower than about 3 wingbeats can meet the measured 60 ms recovery at any gain - the haltere loop is inside that boundary and the visual loop is well outside it. Three weaknesses, all stated in the file: 18 of 24 parameters are assumed rather than sourced, because the journals holding the measured flight numbers were unreachable; the stroke plane is horizontal, which removes by construction the drag-based weight support Fry et al. measured in real hovering flies; and the intact model recovers in 13 ms where a real fly takes under 60, so it is OPTIMISTIC about control and understates rather than overstates what deleting a haltere costs. The delay-versus-gain trade-off it reports is also not new - Elzinga, Dickson & Dickinson 2011 measured it on a dynamically scaled robotic fly - so this is a re-derivation whose value is that it is calibrated against an independently measured recovery time.

data.headline: Redistributing the SAME total wing area over four wings does not fly: 0.46 body weights against 1.00. That is the result to start from, because it is geometry rather than biology - lift scales with the SECOND MOMENT of wing area, so splitting one wing into two smaller ones at constant aspect ratio loses more than half of it, and no contested biological parameter enters. Adding a second DRIVEN pair on top, at double total area, does buy lift - 1.83 body weights - at 2.00 times the mass-specific mechanical power. The configuration the literature actually produced, four wings with the T3 pair un-actuated, reaches 0.84 body weights, and it stays below 1 ACROSS THE WHOLE ADMISSIBLE RANGE of the contested fore-hind interference term rather than at one chosen value of it: it would need the undriven pair to HELP the driven pair to get off the ground. The control half is where the design fails outright. After a 20 degree disturbance the haltere-intact model is back inside 2 degrees in 13 ms, a 30 ms visual loop given its own best gain from the same family takes 101 ms, and putting the fast loop's gain on the slow sense is worse still at 144 ms. Sweeping the loop delay and giving every delay the best gain in the family puts the boundary at 3.0 wingbeats, about 14 ms: a loop slower than that cannot meet the measured recovery at ANY gain. The haltere loop is inside that boundary and the visual loop is well outside it. You cannot buy back a deleted rate gyro by turning up the gain on a slower sense - and note that this model recovers in 13 ms where a real fly takes under 60 ms, so it is OPTIMISTIC about control and understates what deleting a haltere costs.

model.kind: quasi-steady blade-element aerodynamics coupled to a one-axis attitude model written as a delay-differential equation with saturating control

parameters.name: air density
parameters.source: Handbook value for dry air at 20 C and 101.3 kPa. A physical constant of the medium, not a property of the animal.

parameters.name: body mass
parameters.source: Order-of-magnitude value for Drosophila melanogaster. We did not read a measured body mass from any paper during this session: the full text of Fry et al. 2005 (PMID 15939772) is behind a bot challenge and the PubMed record carries only the abstract. Because every result in part (A) is reported as a RATIO to the two-wing arm, this value sets the scale and cancels from the comparison.

parameters.name: wing length (two-wing wild type)
parameters.source: Order-of-magnitude value for Drosophila. Same provenance problem as body mass. Cancels from the ratios.

parameters.name: mean chord (two-wing wild type)
parameters.source: Chosen to give an aspect ratio near 3.6, which is the usual range for dipteran wings. Not read from a paper.

parameters.name: wingbeat frequency
parameters.source: Order-of-magnitude value for Drosophila. Deora, Sane & Sane 2021 (PMID 34783648, full text) establish that this frequency is a property of wing-thorax RESONANCE rather than a free parameter - clipping the wings raises it 'by as much as 90 Hz' - which is why the four-wing arms below hold it fixed rather than letting the model choose it.

parameters.name: stroke amplitude (peak to peak)
parameters.source: About 149 degrees. Within the range usually quoted for hovering flies. Not read from a paper during this session.

parameters.name: mid-stroke angle of attack
parameters.source: 45 degrees is the angle that maximises CL_MAX*sin(2a); choosing it makes the baseline arm as generous as the model allows, which biases the comparison AGAINST the claim that four wings help.

parameters.name: profile drag coefficient at zero angle of attack
parameters.source: Fry et al. 2005 (PMID 15939772, abstract) state that prior time-averaged models underestimated the mean profile drag coefficient 'two- to threefold'; we therefore do not use a small value, but we did not read their number, so this is assumed.

parameters.name: drag coefficient at 90 degrees angle of attack
parameters.source: A flat plate broadside in this Reynolds regime. Not read from a paper.

parameters.name: mass of one wild-type wing, as a fraction of body mass
parameters.source: Insect wings are a small fraction of body mass. Sets the inertial power term and the added moment of inertia of a passive extra wing pair.

parameters.name: body moment of inertia, as m_body * (0.4 * R_wing)^2
parameters.source: Radius of gyration of the body taken as 0.4 of wing length. Sets the absolute angular accelerations; cancels from the configuration ratios except through the ADDED inertia of extra wings, which is the effect the comparison is about.

parameters.name: differential stroke amplitude available for control
parameters.source: Fry, Sayaman & Dickinson 2003 (PMID 12702878, abstract) report that a fly 'generates rapid turns with surprisingly subtle modifications in wing motion'. 10% is our reading of 'subtle'; the number is assumed, and control authority scales linearly in it, so it cancels from every ratio between configurations.

parameters.name: elastic storage of wing inertial energy
parameters.source: Set to zero, i.e. no elastic return of wing kinetic energy. This is the pessimistic end and it is the end that penalises the configurations with MORE wing mass, so it is stated rather than hidden. The perfect-storage bound is emitted alongside every power number.

parameters.name: chord distribution exponent (beta shape, both sides)
parameters.source: c(r) proportional to r^p (1-r)^p, normalised to the mean chord. A smooth insect-like planform. A shape, not a measurement.

parameters.name: passive angular-rate damping time constant
parameters.source: Hedrick, Cheng & Deng 2009 (PMID 19359586, abstract) establish that flapping fliers experience 'substantial damping of angular velocity through a passive mechanism termed flapping counter-torque' and that isometrically scaled animals 'experience similar damping on a per-wingbeat time scale'. We take the CONCEPT and the per-wingbeat scaling from them; the number 8 is ours and is assumed. It is swept.

parameters.name: haltere feedback delay
parameters.source: Fayyazuddin & Dickinson 1996 (PMID 8756451, abstract) report that haltere afferents provide 'direct, electrotonic input to a steering motor neuron', i.e. a monosynaptic, non-spiking path. One wingbeat (4.5 ms here) is our stand-in for 'as fast as this animal can be'; the value is assumed. It is swept.

parameters.name: visual feedback delay
parameters.source: Visual flight reflexes are slower than haltere reflexes; Sherman & Dickinson 2003 (PMID 12477899) compare the two modalities directly. We did not read a latency from that paper, so the number is assumed. It is swept, and the qualitative result (a slow loop cannot replace a fast one) holds across the whole sweep.

parameters.name: recovery band
parameters.source: Ristroph et al. 2010 (PMID 20194789, abstract): flies 'return to their original orientation ... recover their heading to within 2 deg in < 60 ms' after an applied torque impulse.

parameters.name: recovery time to be matched
parameters.source: Same sentence of Ristroph et al. 2010 (PMID 20194789, abstract). This is the independent target the intact model is tested against; it was not used to fit anything.

parameters.name: size of the attitude perturbation used for the headline recovery test
parameters.source: Ristroph et al. describe 'gentle disturbances' but the abstract does not give the magnitude and we could not read the paper, so we could not match it. Recovery time to a FIXED angular band depends on perturbation size, so this study sweeps the perturbation and reports the whole curve rather than one number.

parameters.name: aerodynamic interference penalty on a trailing wing pair
parameters.source: The sign of this term is genuinely contested. Usherwood & Lehmann 2008 (PMID 18477538) report that in dragonflies the PHASING of fore- and hindwings 'can improve aerodynamic efficiency by removing swirl', i.e. a NEGATIVE penalty is attainable; Lai et al. 2020 (PMID 33075754) study wing-wing interaction in damselflies. We sweep this parameter from -0.10 (beneficial, dragonfly-like phasing) to +0.40 and report the whole range.

parameters.name: closed-loop natural period, in multiples of that loop's own delay
parameters.source: The gain rule is a FAMILY, not a value, and it is swept. Each control pathway is then given the member of the family that minimises ITS OWN recovery time, which maximally favours the slow pathway and removes any suspicion that the fast loop wins because it was tuned better. HISTORY, recorded rather than deleted: the first version of this study declared a single value, 4, on the textbook rule of thumb that a delayed loop's natural period should be about four times its delay. That is wrong for a second-order loop - it puts omega_n*tau at pi/2, which is the stability boundary - and every arm, including the intact one, chattered at about 2 degrees for ever and failed the recovery control. Rather than pick a different single number after seeing that failure, which is exactly the move that turns a control into a fit, the rule became a sweep.

parameters.name: standard gravity
parameters.source: Defined value of standard gravity.

parameters.name: maximum lift coefficient CL_MAX
parameters.source: THE ONE CALIBRATED PARAMETER. Chosen so the two-wing wild-type arm produces exactly body weight at the nominal kinematics, which makes every other configuration a prediction relative to it. Its value lands inside the range usually quoted for a translating insect wing with a leading-edge vortex, which is a weak consistency check and not a measurement.

model.fitted_to: the two-wing wild-type arm supporting exactly body weight; declared before the run as D1. The control gains are NOT fitted: they follow the declared delay-based rule D5.

controls.C5_direction_of_the_miss: The intact model recovers FASTER than the animal Ristroph et al. measured, not slower. That is the direction that makes the model optimistic about control, which weakens rather than strengthens the page's conclusion that deleting halteres is costly.
controls.note: A first version of the attitude model used RATE feedback alone. It damped the rotation and then held the body at a constant 4.5 degree heading error for ever, so C5 failed at every perturbation size. That is the correct behaviour of a rate loop and the wrong model of an animal that returns to its original heading, so the controller was changed to a delayed PD loop and the failure is recorded rather than deleted.

configurations.name: two_wing_wild_type
configurations.note: The animal as it is. The calibration arm: lift/weight is 1 by construction, so read every other row against this one.

configurations.name: four_wing_area_conserved
configurations.note: Redistribute the SAME total wing area over four wings, all of them driven. This is the fair version of 'add wings' and the one a designer would actually propose. Note that lift scales with the SECOND moment of wing area, not with area, so splitting one wing into two smaller ones loses lift even before any interference.

configurations.name: four_wing_area_doubled
configurations.note: Bolt on a second full-size pair and drive it. The most generous reading of 'would it fly better'. The cost is power and inertia.

configurations.name: four_wing_T3_unactuated
configurations.note: The configuration the LITERATURE actually produced. Fernandes et al. 1994 (PMID 7874495): in abx bx3 pbx flies 'the adults have two pairs of wings, but the homeotically transformed T3 (HT3) has only rudimentary indirect flight muscles'. Roy et al. 1997 (PMID 9094307) give the cause - Antp is still expressed in the mesoderm of the transformed segment. So the real four-winged fly carries the second pair rather than flying with it.

configurations.name: two_wing_haltere_mass_removed
configurations.note: Identical to wild type in part (A). It is listed so the page can say explicitly that deleting the halteres costs NOTHING in the aerodynamic model, and that everything the halteres do shows up only in part (B).

interference_sweep.note: Negative values mean the trailing pair GAINS lift, which Usherwood & Lehmann 2008 (PMID 18477538) report is attainable in dragonflies at the right fore-hind phase. The sweep is reported whole because the sign is contested.

figures.alt: Four panels of bar charts comparing two-wing wild type against three four-wing configurations: mean vertical force over body weight with a line marking the threshold below which the animal does not fly, mechanical power relative to wild type, roll control authority relative to wild type, and a line plot sweeping the contested fore-hind interference term across all four configurations
figures.caption: Simulation. Quasi-steady blade-element model. Wild type is the single calibrated arm, so its lift is 1.00 by construction and every other bar is a prediction against it. Four wings at the same TOTAL area lose more than half the lift, because lift goes with the second moment of wing area rather than with area: splitting one wing into two smaller ones is a geometric loss before any biology enters. The rightmost panel sweeps the fore-hind interference term rather than fixing it, because the literature disagrees about its sign - dragonfly phasing can make it negative, i.e. helpful.

figures.alt: Three panels. Left, simulated body angle against time after a twenty degree disturbance for four control arms, with a shaded two degree recovery band and a line at sixty milliseconds. Middle, recovery time against disturbance size for three arms on log axes. Right, the best recovery time achievable at each feedback delay, rising roughly linearly, with vertical lines marking the haltere loop and the visual loop and a horizontal line at the measured sixty milliseconds
figures.caption: Simulation. One-axis attitude model with saturating control. The 60 ms / 2 degree line is the only measured quantity on this figure: Ristroph et al. report that disturbed fruit flies recover their heading to within 2 degrees in under 60 ms. In the right-hand panel every delay is given the BEST gain in the declared family, so no loop is handicapped by its tuning - and the best achievable recovery still crosses the measured line at about 3 wingbeats. limbless-mouse.status: design space, mapped and partly simulated

Each carries its own controls, its refinement arm, and a statement of what it does not establish.

schematic.intro: All of this happens in one structure over about two days of mouse development. The routes below are not interchangeable genes; they are interventions at different places in that structure, and that is why they give different animals.
schematic.title: Where each family of routes acts on the limb bud
schematic.desc: On the left, a schematic limb bud projecting from the body wall, with the apical ectodermal ridge along its distal rim, the zone of polarising activity at its posterior base and the progenitor mesenchyme between them. On the right, the maintenance loop drawn as a circuit of four nodes: SHH activates GREM1, GREM1 inhibits BMP, BMP inhibits FGF, and FGF activates SHH. Six numbered pins mark where the routes on this page act; each one is named in the list under this figure.
schematic.caption: Schematic, not a measurement and not to scale.

pins.name: Limb-field induction
pins.note: Tbx5 for the forelimb, Tbx4 and Pitx1 for the hindlimb, Meis1/2 proximally. Remove the field and nothing starts at all.

pins.name: ZPA and its ZRS enhancer
pins.note: Shh is switched on in the ZPA by the ZRS, which sits about a megabase away inside an intron of Lmbr1. This is the cis-regulatory route: edit the switch, not the gene.

pins.name: Ridge induction
pins.note: Fgf10 from the mesenchyme and Wnt3 / β-catenin in the ectoderm raise the apical ectodermal ridge. Lose it and there is no limb at all — this is the amelia route.

pins.name: Ridge maintenance
pins.note: The ridge itself: p63, Fgf4 and Fgf8, or physical ablation. The bud starts and then stops, which is truncation rather than absence.

pins.name: Skeletal patterning
pins.note: BMP–SOX9–WNT sets how many elements the field makes and how far apart. A small enough field makes none.

pins.name: The maintenance loop
pins.note: SHH → GREM1 ⊣ BMP ⊣ FGF → SHH. Break any arm and the bud stops being held open, whichever arm you break.

limbless-mouse.goal: A judge asked whether we could make a limbless mouse. Rather than answer with one gene, map the whole design space: every route we can source, at every scale, with what each one would actually produce.
limbless-mouse.summary: There is no single answer. Published mouse genetics already contains alleles that remove limbs entirely, alleles that truncate them, and alleles that take one limb pair and leave the other. They sit at different scales and they are not interchangeable. This page lays the routes out side by side, runs the models we can run on three of them, and says plainly where the chain between scales is uncalibrated.

answer.headline: Yes, several ways — and they do not give you the same animal.
paragraphs: The honest answer to “could you make a limbless mouse?” is that the mouse literature already contains more than one way, and the first question back is which phenotype is wanted. Complete absence of all four limbs (amelia) is the Fgf10-null phenotype, and in humans the WNT3 Q83X tetra-amelia phenotype: the apical ectodermal ridge never forms, so there is no limb at all. Truncation is a different outcome reached by a different lesion: the limb bud starts, the SHH–GREM1–FGF loop fails to sustain it, and a stunted proximal element is left behind.

The sharpest precedent for getting there by editing regulation rather than by deleting a gene is Kvon et al. 2016. Replacing the mouse ZRS — the limb enhancer of Shh, about a megabase away inside an intron of Lmbr1 — with the king cobra ortholog abolished limb-bud Shh expression and truncated both limb pairs, while the human and coelacanth orthologs in the same assay gave normal limbs. And the 17 base pairs are not an association: Kvon et al. put that stretch, carrying an ETS site, back into the python ZRS, knocked that engineered allele into mice, and got normal limbs. Four ortholog knock-ins and one resurrected allele is the whole causal dataset, which is small — but it is a causal one. That is the resolution at which this is a design problem rather than a knockout.

If the goal is a viable adult animal rather than an embryonic phenotype, the realistic route is one limb pair, not four: a conditional Tbx5 allele for the forelimb, Tbx4 or Pitx1 for the hindlimb, switched after the body plan is laid down. Tetra-amelia alleles are generally severe and often lethal for reasons that have nothing to do with limbs.
And if the point is the mechanism rather than the mouse, the first thing a reviewer will ask for in 2026 is a limb-bud explant or organoid, not an animal. That route is on this page too.
answer.precision_note: Truncation is not amelia, and a page that blurs them is answering a question nobody asked. Every route below states which of the two — or which of micromelia, digit loss, or one-pair loss — it predicts.

scales.label: Molecular / sequence
scales.blurb: Change non-coding DNA and leave every protein intact. This is the layer where a limb can be removed without touching anything else the gene does, and it is the layer evolution used in snakes and sticklebacks. It is also the only layer a genome language model emits a score for.

scales.label: Gene / coding
scales.blurb: Delete or break the protein. The phenotypes here are the strongest and best documented, and most of them kill the animal for a reason that has nothing to do with limbs - lung, kidney, allantois, heart. The gene scale tells you what a node does; it rarely gives you an animal.

scales.label: Cell / signalling centre
scales.blurb: Remove or silence the AER or the ZPA as structures, rather than the genes that specify them. This is where the subject started, with a scalpel, and it is where the timing question is posed most directly: cut the ridge off later and you get more limb.

scales.label: Tissue / maintenance loop
scales.blurb: The circuit that decides how long the bud keeps growing: a SHH-GREM1-FGF loop that is self-promoting AND self-terminating, because rising FGF activity represses Grem1. It sets limb SIZE and when outgrowth stops. Nobody has shown that triggering it early removes a limb, and the page says so.

scales.label: Pattern formation
scales.blurb: The reaction-diffusion system that decides how many digits the autopod carries and how they are spaced: a BMP-SOX9-WNT Turing network whose wavelength distal Hox dose sets. This explains autopod FORM. Both published knobs move it toward MORE digits, not fewer, so nothing here has been shown to explain limb absence.

scales.label: Developmental timing
scales.blurb: Apply the lesion when you choose rather than at fertilisation. This is the scale that converts lethal mutants into viable animals and binary genotypes into ordered series, and it is where our recommendation sits. The same Tbx4 deletion gives blocked outgrowth, proximal hypoplasia, or nothing at all, depending only on the hour.

scales.label: Organism / evolutionary comparative
scales.blurb: Four independent natural limb losses - snakes, limb-reduced skinks, cetaceans, stickleback pelvis - solved by at least three different mechanisms at three different layers. They are the ground truth this subject has and ours does not, and they are the reason to present a design space instead of an answer.

scales.label: Non-animal / in vitro
scales.blurb: Budoids, human iPSC limb-bud mesenchyme, limb-bud explants, recombinant limbs and trunk-like structures. The route a modern reviewer asks about first, the route with the best welfare case, and the route whose honest limit is that no dish currently makes a limb.

chain.title: The chain across scales, and where it is not calibrated
chain.intro: The three models on this page are not independent demonstrations. They are meant to be read as one chain, and the chain has two junctions we refuse to call calibrated.

links.note: The sequence analysis measures divergence and motif content. It does not predict enhancer activity. Mapping an allele onto a fraction of wild-type Shh output is a scenario parameter, not a calibrated transfer.
This junction is inside the SHH–GREM1–FGF model, so it is at least explicit: the model says how a reduction in Shh production shortens the window in which FGF stays above threshold.
A shorter outgrowth window means a smaller paddle, but the model has no geometry. Converting one to the other needs a growth law we have not fitted.

This junction is inside the Turing model, which gives a critical domain size of about 0.94 ± 0.10 of the pattern's own wavelength — and finds that every route to zero elements in it is the same geometric condition, the Turing-permissive region having to be at least about one wavelength across.

chain.verdict: Two of the four junctions are within a single model and are explicit. Two cross between models and have no calibration behind them, so the end-to-end statement — “this allele gives that many digits” — is refused. The chain is a map of what would have to be measured, not a prediction.

not_claimed: No mouse was made, no embryo was used, and no wet-lab experiment was run for this page.
The three computational studies are simulations and a sequence analysis. None is an observation, and none is calibrated to a measured mouse limb bud.
No route on this page is a protocol. Each names published evidence and what would have to be done; none has been attempted here.
The sequence analysis is correlational over a handful of orthologs. It is not a predictor of enhancer activity and must not be used as one.
A threshold in a model is not a threshold in an embryo.

closing.title: Why this is on a design platform and not in a review article

link.text: The longer written answer in the repository

closing.text: The useful thing here is not the list — a specialist could write the list. It is that every row carries its evidence level, every junction between scales carries a refusal or a label, and the three models can be re-run from the repository. The question “can you make a limbless mouse?” has a dozen answers whose differences only show up when you are forced to say which phenotype, at which scale, with what evidence, and at what cost. That is what this workspace is for.

routes.title: Replace the mouse ZRS with a snake ortholog (king cobra or Burmese python)
routes.mechanism: The ZRS is a limb-specific enhancer of Shh sitting ~1 Mb from the Shh promoter inside Lmbr1 intron 5, and it is the sole driver of Shh expression in the posterior limb bud mesenchyme. Snake ZRS orthologs have accumulated substitutions that destroy the transcription-factor binding sites the enhancer needs, so an otherwise wild-type mouse carrying a snake ZRS makes no limb-bud Shh. Every protein in the genome is left intact; only 1.3 kb of non-coding DNA changes.
routes.intervention: CRISPR/Cas9 homology-directed replacement of the functionally critical 1.3 kb ZRS core with the same-length orthologous sequence from king cobra (Ophiophagus hannah) or Burmese python (Python bivittatus). Kvon et al. did exactly this in FVB mice with a matched-littermate design.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Severe TRUNCATION of both fore- and hindlimbs, not amelia. The cobra knock-in gives complete loss of limb-bud Shh and a phenotype indistinguishable from deleting the enhancer outright; the proximal skeleton is present. The python knock-in is slightly milder: most elements distal to the stylopod:zeugopod junction are severely affected, but 2-3 rudimentary digits form in the forelimb and a slightly enlarged ossification resembling a rudimentary zeugopod appears, attributed to very weak residual Shh transcript detectable only after prolonged in-situ development.

evidence.cite: Kvon EZ et al. 2016, Cell 167:633-642.e11, 'Progressive Loss of Function in a Limb Enhancer during Snake Evolution'
evidence.finding: Replacing the mouse ZRS with the cobra ortholog 'resulted in a complete loss of [Shh] expression and a truncated limb phenotype, affecting both the fore- and hindlimbs, that is indistinguishable from the phenotype caused by deletion of the mouse enhancer'. The python ortholog gave 'a similar but a slightly milder phenotype ... 2-3 rudimentary digits in the forelimb'. Human and coelacanth orthologs rescued fully developed limbs.

routes.reversibility: Not reversible in the animal: this is a germline sequence change fixed at the zygote. It IS reversible at the design stage - reintroducing 17 bp restores normal limbs (see mol-zrs-e1-ets-site), which makes the allele series itself a dose knob rather than a switch.
routes.lethality_risk: Low. ZRS-null mice are alive and of comparable body size at two weeks of age; Kvon et al. photographed them. Mouse ZRS reporter assays show no reproducible activity outside the limb and ZRS deletion studies report no phenotypes beyond limb defects, so there is no known non-limb organ requirement.
routes.specificity: Limb only, both pairs, posterior-distal. It removes the autopod and zeugopod and spares the stylopod and girdle. It does not touch lung, kidney, allantois, neural tube or craniofacial structures.
routes.difficulty: low-to-medium. The exact sgRNA, donor design, homology arms and genotyping primers are published; the line already exists in at least one lab. Cost is a standard CRISPR knock-in campaign plus a mouse colony.
routes.what_we_would_run:
Score the published ortholog series with a genome language model (we have an Evo 2 7B pipeline that has produced one real paired result on zebrafish regulatory windows) and ask whether the model's ranking reproduces the measured ranking: human ~ coelacanth (normal) > python (weak residual) > cobra (none). Pre-register the prediction. Controls: dinucleotide shuffles and GC-matched random windows, as in the run we already did.

STUDY: The study `zrs-conservation` IS this route's assay: it is the ZRS ortholog panel, and the measured knock-in ranking (human ~ coelacanth normal > python weak residual > cobra none) is the answer key any score would be checked against.
open_questions: Does a sequence model separate cobra from coelacanth, given that coelacanth shares LESS sequence identity with human ZRS (57%) than python does (59%) yet behaves like wild type? This is the single sharpest test in the dataset and it is an explicit identity-versus-function dissociation.
Boa ZRS retained ZPA reporter activity but was never taken to knock-in, so the 'ordered series' is four knock-in phenotypes plus reporter data, not a uniform assay.

routes.title: Delete the ZRS outright
routes.mechanism: Removing the enhancer removes the only known driver of limb-bud Shh. Shh protein is still made everywhere else it is normally made (notochord, floor plate, gut), so the animal has no midline, neural-tube or axial defect. This is the cleanest available dissociation between 'Shh the gene' and 'Shh in the limb'.
routes.intervention: CRISPR/Cas9 deletion of the 1,324 bp ZRS (mm10 chr5:29,314,497-29,315,820), or the earlier targeted deletion of the conserved intronic module. Both alleles exist.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Truncation of both limbs with a surviving proximal skeleton. At E18.5 the forelimb humerus, radius and ulna appear fused and no recognisable autopod is present; the hindlimb zeugopod is severely reduced and the autopod is represented by a single rudimentary digit. Animals survive to at least two weeks with body size comparable to wild type.

evidence.cite: Kvon EZ et al. 2016, Cell 167:633-642.e11
evidence.finding: Figure S3E-F: 'Gross phenotypes of two week old ZRS(+/+) (top) and ZRS(-/-) (bottom) mice. The body sizes are comparable, but ZRS(-/-) mice have truncated limbs.' Skeletal detail as described above.

evidence.cite: Sagai T et al. 2005, Development 132:797-803, 'Elimination of a long-range cis-regulatory module causes complete loss of limb-specific Shh expression and truncation of the mouse limb'
evidence.finding: Targeted deletion of the conserved intronic sequence gives 'a complete loss of Shh expression in the limb bud and degeneration of skeletal elements distal to the stylopod/zygopod junction'.

routes.reversibility: None in the animal. Germline, constitutive.
routes.lethality_risk: Low; this is the only route in the whole design space with a published photograph of a limb-reduced mouse alive at two weeks and of normal body size.
routes.specificity: Limb only, both pairs. Spares girdle and stylopod.
routes.difficulty: low. Two independent alleles published, one of them CRISPR-made specifically to exclude neo-cassette and background effects.
routes.what_we_would_run:
Nothing new computationally - this is the reference phenotype everything else is scored against, and it is the anchor for the honest claim that 'limbless mouse' in the ZRS literature means limb-REDUCED and viable, not amelia.

STUDY: `zrs-conservation` bears on this route as its anchor: the ZRS-null is the wild-type-to-null endpoint the ortholog series is read against, and it is the reference phenotype for the whole molecular scale.
open_questions: Welfare: a viable animal with truncated limbs is the ethically harder case precisely because it lives. See the welfare section.
No published long-term (adult, >2 week) husbandry or behavioural data was found in our search.

routes.title: Edit the single E1 ETS binding site - a 17 bp switch
routes.mechanism: A 17 bp deletion overlapping the E1 ETS1 recognition motif is the only sequence present in all examined limbed vertebrates and fish and absent from all examined snakes. Reintroducing those 17 bp into an otherwise-python ZRS restores full enhancer activity in the posterior limb-bud mesenchyme and rescues normal limb development in the mouse. Conversely the site is the smallest known handle on the whole system.
routes.intervention: CRISPR knock-in of a 1,341 bp synthetic 'resurrected python' allele (python ZRS plus the 17 bp lizard sequence) in place of the mouse ZRS; or the reciprocal, removing the 17 bp from an otherwise wild-type mouse ZRS.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Reintroduction direction: NORMAL limbs. Removal direction: Kvon et al. state that loss of the E1 motif in the mouse ZRS alone is NOT sufficient to alter limb-bud expression, and boa ZRS is active despite lacking both E0 and E1, so deleting E1 in mouse is predicted to give normal or near-normal limbs. Do not state that removing 17 bp from a mouse removes its limbs; the literature says the opposite.

evidence.cite: Kvon EZ et al. 2016, Cell 167:633-642.e11
evidence.finding: 'reintroduction of 17 bp of sequence alone was sufficient to reinstate full enhancer activity' and knock-in mice with the modified python allele 'had normal limbs'. Separately: 'the loss of E1 motif in mouse ZRS is not sufficient to alter limb bud expression' and boa ZRS is active despite lacking E0 and E1, so 'loss of these motifs alone cannot explain ZRS deactivation in snake lineage'.

routes.reversibility: This is the one asymmetric, directional result in the design space: the 17 bp is sufficient to RESTORE function on a degraded background but not sufficient to DESTROY function on a healthy one. Context-dependence of this kind is exactly what a per-nucleotide additive sequence model will get wrong.
routes.lethality_risk: None beyond the background allele.
routes.specificity: Limb only.
routes.difficulty: low. Published allele, published sequence.
routes.what_we_would_run:
Ask a genome language model for the effect of the 17 bp indel in BOTH directions and on BOTH backgrounds (mouse ZRS minus 17 bp; python ZRS plus 17 bp). A model that reports a symmetric effect has failed a test with a known answer. This is a cheap, pre-registerable, falsifiable experiment, and the published asymmetry means we know the right answer before scoring.

STUDY: `zrs-conservation` bears on this route directly, and this is the sharpest test in it: the 17 bp E1 indel has a published ASYMMETRIC effect, so a model scored on that panel has a known-in-advance right answer to fail.
open_questions: Kvon et al. explicitly say ETS-site loss alone cannot explain snake ZRS deactivation and point at homeodomain motifs with a similar snake-specific substitution increase. So E1 is necessary-in-context, not the mechanism.

routes.title: Design a graded ZRS hypomorphic allelic series from the in-vivo variant panel
routes.mechanism: Nearly a thousand human ZRS variants have been assayed in vivo in a high-throughput mouse reporter, and selected variants were confirmed in knock-in mice. That panel is a measured sequence-to-activity map over the exact element that sets limb-bud Shh. In principle one can pick combinations that place enhancer activity at a chosen point between wild type and null and so dial the degree of limb reduction.
routes.intervention: Select variant combinations from the published panel, knock them in, and read out skeletal phenotype at E18.5.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Unknown and the honest answer is that the published panel points the WRONG WAY for this purpose. Kvon et al. 2020 assayed an enhancer 'repeatedly linked to polydactyly' and the knock-in confirmations were of variants that CAUSE polydactyly - a gain of ectopic anterior activity, i.e. extra digits, not fewer. A graded loss-of-function series would have to be designed and tested; it does not exist in that dataset.

evidence.cite: Kvon EZ et al. 2020, Cell 180:1262-1271.e15, 'Comprehensive In Vivo Interrogation Reveals Phenotypic Impact of Human Enhancer Variants'
evidence.finding: '71% of all rare non-coding variants previously proposed as causal lead to reporter gene expression in a pattern consistent with their pathogenic role. Variants observed to alter enhancer activity were further confirmed to cause polydactyly in knockin mice.' Combinatorial and single-nucleotide mutagenesis covered all positions of the enhancer.

evidence.cite: Gurnett CA et al. 2007, Am J Med Genet A 143A:27-32, 'Two novel point mutations in the long-range SHH enhancer in three families with triphalangeal thumb and preaxial polydactyly'
evidence.finding: Point mutations within the ZRS (bp 621, bp 739 of a 774 bp conserved core in LMBR1 intron 5) segregate with triphalangeal thumb and preaxial polydactyly; both alter putative Cdx binding sites. A 5'-end mutation was associated with a milder phenotype and 82% penetrance.

routes.lethality_risk: Low, by analogy with the deletion.
routes.specificity: Limb only.
routes.difficulty: high, because the loss-of-function side of the map is not the side that was measured. Building it means a new in-vivo panel.
routes.what_we_would_run:
Score the Kvon 2020 panel and report rank correlation against the published in-vivo calls - but label it for what it is: a benchmark on the POLYDACTYLY (gain) direction, used as a proxy for whether the model has any grip on this element at all. Reporting it as a limb-loss benchmark would be a category error.

STUDY: `zrs-conservation` bears on this route, but only on its gain-of-function half - the panel it would be scored against was assayed for polydactyly, not limb reduction, and that has to be stated wherever the number is reported.
open_questions: Is a model that ranks gain-of-function ZRS variants well also good at loss-of-function ZRS variants? Nothing in the literature we read answers this, and assuming transfer is exactly the kind of assumption that has failed before.

routes.title: Break the CTCF-mediated contact between the ZRS and the SHH promoter
routes.mechanism: The ZRS acts across ~1 Mb, and that action depends on physical contact. Three CTCF sites inside a 12 kb interval of LMBR1 mediate the ZRS-to-SHH-promoter interaction. Homozygous deletion of that interval in humans causes acheiropodia, congenital limb truncation, and the interval does not itself function as an enhancer - the lesion is architectural, not transcriptional.
routes.intervention: Delete or mutate the CTCF sites that anchor the ZRS-promoter loop, leaving the enhancer sequence intact.
routes.predicted_phenotype: In humans: acheiropodia - congenital truncation of hands and feet. In mouse: NO APPARENT ABNORMALITY. This route is the design space's clearest documented failure of species transfer.

evidence.cite: Ushiki A et al. 2021, Nat Commun 12:2282, 'Deletion of CTCF sites in the SHH locus alters enhancer-promoter interactions and leads to acheiropodia'
evidence.finding: Fine-mapped the acheiropodia region to 12 kb; it does not function as an enhancer. Three CTCF sites mediate the ZRS-SHH promoter interaction, substituted by centromeric sites in disease. 'Mouse knockouts of the orthologous 12 kb sequence have no apparent abnormalities, showcasing the challenges in modelling CTCF alterations in animal models due to inherent motif differences between species.'

routes.lethality_risk: Not applicable in mouse (no phenotype). In humans acheiropodia is compatible with life.
routes.specificity: Would be limb-restricted if it worked, because the contact being broken is the limb enhancer's.
routes.difficulty: high, and currently unsolved: nobody has engineered a mouse allele that reproduces the human architectural lesion. It would require re-deriving the CTCF motif arrangement for the mouse locus rather than copying the human deletion.
routes.what_we_would_run: Encode this as an explicit REFUSAL in our cross-scale coupling layer: a human-to-mouse transfer of a CTCF-motif-dependent claim is not composable, and the layer should say so with the Ushiki result as the stated reason rather than emitting a score. This is a one-record change and it is the kind of thing the layer exists for. No study on this page bears on this route; naming one would stretch the link past what it supports.
open_questions: Which mouse CTCF sites would have to be removed to phenocopy acheiropodia? Nobody has published an answer.
Would a sequence model trained on human data flag the mouse orthologous deletion as benign? If it does, that is the correct answer and worth demonstrating.

routes.title: Move a TAD boundary so the limb enhancer cluster drives the wrong gene
routes.mechanism: Limb enhancers are confined to a topologically associating domain by CTCF-associated boundaries. Deletions, inversions and duplications that disrupt those boundaries let a cluster of limb enhancers contact a promoter it should never reach, producing ectopic limb expression of the wrong gene. The rewiring occurs only when the variant disrupts a CTCF-associated boundary - the structural change, not the sequence content, is the lesion.
routes.intervention: CRISPR engineering of deletions, inversions or duplications at a TAD boundary, modelled on the human WNT6/IHH/EPHA4/PAX3 rearrangements, which were reproduced as mouse alleles.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Limb MALFORMATION of a type set by which gene is misexpressed (the published human conditions at this locus are brachydactyly, polydactyly and syndactyly) - not limb loss. This route is in the design space because it is the general architectural mechanism and because it is mouse-validated, not because it has been shown to remove a limb.

evidence.cite: Lupianez DG et al. 2015, Cell 161:1012-1025, 'Disruptions of topological chromatin domains cause pathogenic rewiring of gene-enhancer interactions'
evidence.finding: Distinct human limb malformations are caused by deletions, inversions or duplications altering the TAD-spanning WNT6/IHH/EPHA4/PAX3 locus; CRISPR mice with corresponding rearrangements showed ectopic promoter-noncoding contacts and ectopic limb expression. 'This rewiring occurred only if the variant disrupted a CTCF-associated boundary domain.'

routes.lethality_risk: Locus-dependent; the published alleles are viable.
routes.specificity: Depends entirely on which domain is broken. A boundary move is a blunt instrument: it changes everything in the domain, not one enhancer-promoter pair.
routes.difficulty: high. Large structural variants are harder to make and harder to genotype than a 1.3 kb replacement, and the outcome is not predictable from sequence alone.
routes.what_we_would_run: Nothing yet. A sequence model that scores 1 kb windows has no representation of a megabase-scale boundary, so this route is a good argument for why 'score the enhancer' is not the same as 'predict the phenotype', and it belongs on the page as that argument. No study on this page bears on this route; naming one would stretch the link past what it supports.
open_questions: Can any current sequence model predict the direction of a boundary-disruption phenotype? We found no evidence that one can, and our search did not cover the chromatin-model literature.

routes.title: Delete the Pitx1 hindlimb enhancer - nature's own cis-regulatory limb removal
routes.mechanism: In threespine stickleback, pelvic (hindlimb-homologue) loss has evolved repeatedly through deletion of a tissue-specific enhancer of Pitx1. Pitx1 null alleles are lethal in laboratory animals; the enhancer deletion is not, and it carries molecular signatures of positive selection. This is the proof of principle that evolution solves 'remove an appendage without killing the animal' by cis-regulation, not by knockout.
routes.intervention: Identify and delete the mouse orthologous hindlimb-specific Pitx1 enhancer. The stickleback element is characterised; the mouse equivalent would have to be mapped, which is work, not a copy.
routes.predicted_phenotype: In stickleback: pelvic reduction/loss, viable, naturally selected. In mouse: UNKNOWN and not to be asserted. The best-supported expectation is a hindlimb-restricted phenotype milder than the Pitx1 null (which gives hindlimb hypoplasia, not absence), but we found no published mouse Pitx1 limb-enhancer deletion.

evidence.cite: Chan YF et al. 2010, Science 327:302-5, 'Adaptive evolution of pelvic reduction in sticklebacks by recurrent deletion of a Pitx1 enhancer'
evidence.finding: Pelvic loss in different natural stickleback populations occurred through regulatory mutations deleting a tissue-specific Pitx1 enhancer. 'Although Pitx1 null mutations are lethal in laboratory animals, Pitx1 regulatory mutations show molecular signatures of positive selection in pelvic-reduced populations.' Deletion is recurrent, possibly from structural features of the locus.

evidence.cite: Lanctot C et al. 1999, Development 126:1805-10, 'Hindlimb patterning and mandible development require the Ptx1 gene'
evidence.finding: Mouse Pitx1 (Ptx1) null: hindlimb development severely impaired but not abolished - ilium and knee cartilage absent, long bones underdeveloped, Tbx4 expression decreased; also loss of proximal mandibular bones. Limb-bud molecular identity is retained.

routes.specificity: Hindlimb only, if the mouse element behaves like the stickleback one. Note the mouse Pitx1 null ALSO loses proximal mandibular bone, so the gene is not hindlimb-exclusive even if the enhancer is.
routes.lethality_risk: Low for an enhancer deletion by the stickleback precedent; high for the null in laboratory animals per Chan et al.
routes.difficulty: high, because the mouse enhancer has to be found first and the Ushiki result (above) is a standing warning that a cis-element's behaviour does not transfer between species.
routes.what_we_would_run: This is the single best test case for a sequence model doing something useful rather than reproducing a known answer: use the model to nominate candidate hindlimb-specific Pitx1 enhancers in mouse, then check the nominations against published limb-bud ATAC/ChIP data. That is a retrieval task with an external answer key, not a self-graded one. No study on this page bears on this route; naming one would stretch the link past what it supports.
open_questions: Is there a single mouse Pitx1 hindlimb enhancer, or distributed redundancy? Enhancer redundancy is the standard reason a cis-deletion gives no phenotype, and we did not search the Pitx1 regulatory-landscape literature.

routes.title: Fgf10 germline null - the canonical tetra-amelia mouse
routes.mechanism: FGF10 is the mesenchymal signal that induces and sustains the apical ectodermal ridge (AER); it acts epistatically upstream of Fgf8, the earliest AER marker. Without it the AER never forms, the ZPA never forms, and the limb bud makes no outgrowth. The same ligand drives branching morphogenesis in lung, so the mouse has no lungs either.
routes.intervention: Germline Fgf10 knockout (two independent lines published, 1998 and 1999).
routes.predicted_phenotype: AMELIA. Fetuses develop to birth with complete absence of both fore- and hindlimbs. The clavicle is unaffected (it is a dermal bone of different origin). Perinatal lethal from complete absence of lungs: the trachea forms, main-stem bronchial formation and all subsequent branching do not.

evidence.cite: Min H et al. 1998, Genes Dev 12:3156-61, 'Fgf-10 is required for both limb and lung development...'
evidence.finding: 'Limb bud initiation was abolished in Fgf-10(-/-) mice. Strikingly, Fgf-10(-/-) fetuses continued to develop until birth, despite the complete absence of both fore- and hindlimbs. Fgf-10 is necessary for apical ectodermal ridge (AER) formation and acts epistatically upstream of Fgf-8.' Perinatal lethality with complete absence of lungs.

evidence.cite: Sekine K et al. 1999, Nat Genet 21:138-41, 'Fgf10 is essential for limb and lung formation'
evidence.finding: 'complete truncation of the fore- and hindlimbs. In Fgf10-/- embryos, limb bud formation was initiated but outgrowth of the limb buds did not occur ... the apical ectodermal ridge (AER) and the zone of polarizing activity (ZPA) did not form'; clavicle formation unaffected; died at birth from lack of lung development.

routes.reversibility: None. Germline, constitutive, and the animal cannot be rescued because the lung defect is independent of the limb defect.
routes.lethality_risk: HIGH and certain: perinatal lethal from lung agenesis. No Fgf10-null mouse has ever drawn a breath, so there is no viable limbless adult by this route.
routes.specificity: Poor. FGF10 is the major ligand for FGFR2b across many organs: Fgf10-null mice also lack thyroid, pituitary and salivary glands, with minor defects in teeth, kidney, hair follicles and digestive organs.
routes.difficulty: low to make, impossible to make viable as a constitutive allele. The conditional version is the route worth proposing (see timing-prx1-creer-fgf10).
routes.what_we_would_run: Nothing computational adds value here; this is the ground-truth amelia phenotype the whole page is calibrated against. If the judge's mice were tetra-amelic AND died at birth, this is the likely mechanism class. No study on this page bears on this route; naming one would stretch the link past what it supports.
open_questions: The two founding papers DISAGREE about whether the limb bud initiates: Min et al. say initiation was abolished; Sekine et al. say bud formation initiated but outgrowth did not occur. We preserve that disagreement rather than reconciling it, and it matters because it decides whether the lesion is in induction or in maintenance.

routes.title: Fgfr2-IIIb (FGFR2b) isoform null - the receptor side of the same axis
routes.mechanism: Fgfr2 is alternatively spliced into IIIb and IIIc isoforms with different ligand specificities and mutually exclusive tissue distributions. FGFR2b is the epithelial receptor that reads mesenchymal FGF10. Removing only IIIb leaves IIIc intact and so removes one arm of the mesenchymal-epithelial dialogue rather than the whole receptor.
routes.intervention: Cre-mediated excision of the IIIb exon, retaining IIIc expression.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Severe limb defects with a distinctive time course: 'development of these structures appears to initiate, but then fails with the tissues undergoing extensive apoptosis'. Viable until birth. Also severe lung and anterior pituitary defects, plus salivary gland, inner ear, tooth, skin and minor skull abnormalities.

evidence.cite: De Moerlooze L et al. 2000, Development 127:483-92, 'An important role for the IIIb isoform of fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2) in mesenchymal-epithelial signalling during mouse organogenesis'
evidence.finding: 'Fibroblast growth factor receptor 2(IIIb) null mice are viable until birth, but have severe defects of the limbs, lung and anterior pituitary gland. The development of these structures appears to initiate, but then fails with the tissues undergoing extensive apoptosis.'

evidence.cite: Ohuchi H et al. 2000, Biochem Biophys Res Commun 277:643-9, 'FGF10 acts as a major ligand for FGF receptor 2 IIIb in mouse multi-organ development'
evidence.finding: Fgf10-null phenotypes closely parallel FGFR2b-deficient phenotypes across many organs (absent thyroid, pituitary, salivary glands), supporting FGF10 as the major FGFR2b ligand in organogenesis.

routes.lethality_risk: High - viable until birth only, with lung and pituitary agenesis.
routes.specificity: Poor; multi-organ, by construction (the whole point of the receptor is that it serves many epithelia).
routes.difficulty: low to make; same viability dead end as Fgf10.
routes.what_we_would_run: Nothing new. This route earns its place by being the mechanistic mirror of Fgf10 and by showing that 'initiates then apoptoses' is a THIRD phenotypic class distinct from both amelia and truncation - a distinction the existing dossier does not draw. No study on this page bears on this route; naming one would stretch the link past what it supports.
open_questions: Is the limb defect in Fgfr2-IIIb nulls the same as the Fgf10 null, or milder because other FGFR2b ligands partially compensate? The abstracts do not settle it and we did not read the bodies.

routes.title: Ectodermal WNT3 / beta-catenin - the human tetra-amelia gene
routes.mechanism: Wnt3 is expressed ubiquitously in limb ectoderm and signals through beta-catenin to establish the AER; beta-catenin is also required continuously to MAINTAIN the ridge once induced. Wnt/beta-catenin sits upstream of BMP signalling in AER establishment and interacts with BMPR1A in dorsoventral patterning. In humans a homozygous nonsense allele of WNT3 causes complete absence of all four limbs.
routes.intervention: Mouse: Wnt3 loss, or conditional removal of beta-catenin from ventral limb ectoderm (before induction to prevent the AER, after induction to make an existing AER disappear). Human: the natural WNT3 Q83X allele.
routes.predicted_phenotype: Human WNT3 Q83X homozygotes: TETRA-AMELIA - complete absence of all four limbs, with craniofacial and urogenital defects. Mouse: AER fails to be established; removing beta-catenin after induction makes an existing AER disappear, giving a later and milder truncation. Note Wnt3-null mice are reported early-lethal, which is why the human allele is the informative one.

evidence.cite: Niemann S et al. 2004, Am J Hum Genet 74:558-63, 'Homozygous WNT3 mutation causes tetra-amelia in a large consanguineous family'
evidence.finding: Homozygous nonsense mutation Q83X in WNT3 in four affected fetuses with autosomal recessive tetra-amelia plus craniofacial and urogenital defects. 'Our findings contrast with the observation of early lethality in mice homozygous for null alleles of Wnt3.' First WNT-gene mutation associated with a Mendelian disorder.

evidence.cite: Barrow JR et al. 2003, Genes Dev 17:394-409, 'Ectodermal Wnt3/beta-catenin signaling is required for the establishment and maintenance of the apical ectodermal ridge'
evidence.finding: Conditional removal of beta-catenin in ventral ectodermal cells is sufficient to elicit the mutant limb phenotype; removing beta-catenin AFTER ridge induction results in the disappearance of the AER. Wnt/beta-catenin lies upstream of BMP in AER establishment.

evidence.cite: Soshnikova N et al. 2003, Genes Dev 17:1963-8, 'Genetic interaction between Wnt/beta-catenin and BMP receptor signaling during formation of the AER and the dorsal-ventral axis in the limb'
